title: Biomedical Signal Analysis
short: An interactive Streamlit dashboard for gait-cycle segmentation, joint kinematics and multi-channel EMG analysis from wearable sensor recordings (foot-switch, joint angle, 9-channel EMG).
problem: A single walking trial produces foot-switch, joint-angle and 9-channel EMG data at once — none of it means anything until it's filtered, segmented into gait cycles and turned into comparable parameters, and doing that by hand for every trial and every muscle doesn't scale.
approach: Built as a multi-page Streamlit dashboard where each sensor stream gets its own processing path: heel/toe force signals go through a Butterworth low-pass filter into heel-strike/toe-off event detection and gait-cycle segmentation; joint angles are normalized per cycle into a mean ± SD ensemble curve per joint; and each EMG channel goes through a Butterworth bandpass filter (20–450 Hz), full-wave rectification, a linear envelope and activation thresholding — with a dedicated STFT page for inspecting any EMG channel's time-frequency content.
result: A working analysis dashboard: upload raw sensor files and get gait events, per-joint kinematic curves, EMG activation timing and amplitude parameters (RMS, MAV, iEMG), and an EMG spectrogram — all from one interface, built as an engineering learning tool rather than a diagnostic device.
tagline: From raw wearable-sensor traces to gait cycles, joint curves and muscle activation.
highlights: Mean ± SD kinematics, RMS / MAV / iEMG
details: The dashboard treats each signal type on its own terms instead of forcing one shared pipeline: a foot-switch just needs a threshold, EMG needs rectification and an envelope before it means anything, and joint angles need per-cycle normalization before they're comparable across strides. Six pages — Gait Parameters, Joint Analysis, Dynamic EMG, EMG Preprocessing, Parameter Table and STFT Analysis — cover the full path from raw sensor file to summary parameters.
learned: Splitting FSR, joint-angle and EMG into three separate but parallel processing paths — instead of one shared pipeline — made it clear how differently each signal type actually needs to be treated before it's usable, and how much of the real work in biomedical signal analysis is choosing the right filter and normalization for each channel, not just running an FFT.

title: Biomedical Signal Time-Frequency Analysis
short: A Streamlit app for exploring how a signal's frequency content changes over time — synthetic, sine or real ECG signals through FFT, STFT and Continuous Wavelet Transform.
problem: A single FFT collapses an entire signal into one static frequency spectrum — it shows that a frequency is present, not when it happens, which hides exactly the kind of transient, time-varying behaviour biomedical signals tend to have.
approach: Built as a Streamlit application with three signal sources — a synthetic four-segment piecewise sinusoid (50→150→250→350 Hz) for visually checking time-frequency resolution, a configurable sine wave, or an ECG signal (simulated via NeuroKit2, or your own recording uploaded as CSV/TXT with automatic column detection and DC-offset removal). Any signal can then be inspected through a selectable window function (Rectangular, Bartlett, Hann, Hamming, Blackman), a global FFT spectrum, a Short-Time Fourier Transform with configurable window length and overlap, and a Continuous Wavelet Transform (Morlet, Mexican Hat, Gaussian) across a chosen scale range — including an interactive 3D time-frequency surface.
result: An interactive comparison tool: the same signal viewed as a time-domain trace, a static FFT spectrum, a 2D STFT spectrogram, a CWT scalogram and a 3D time-frequency surface — including a full demo of uploading a real ECG recording end-to-end. Built to make the trade-off between time resolution and frequency resolution visible instead of purely theoretical.
tagline: One spectrum tells you what's there. A spectrogram tells you when.
details: FFT gives a global view of which frequencies are present but discards when they occur. STFT and CWT sit alongside it specifically to recover that time information — STFT with a fixed window and configurable overlap, CWT with a bank of wavelet scales — so the same signal, including a real uploaded ECG recording, can be compared across three different time-frequency trade-offs (plus a 3D surface view) in one place.
learned: Watching the same signal move through FFT, STFT and CWT made the time-frequency trade-off concrete: STFT's fixed window trades time and frequency resolution uniformly across the signal, while CWT's variable scale gives up some of that uniformity to resolve fast transients and slow trends differently — a distinction that's easy to state and much clearer to actually see once a real, uploaded ECG recording is the thing being analyzed.

title: Blockchain Experiments
short: Hands-on experiments around smart contracts, stablecoins and practical Web3 systems.
problem: Separating useful blockchain primitives from hype requires building and testing ideas directly.
approach: Explore smart contracts, stablecoin mechanics and decentralized application patterns through small experiments.
result: A growing notebook of prototypes, technical notes and questions worth investigating.
tagline: Build the primitive first. Debate the narrative later.
details: This is intentionally a living lab. The goal is to understand what blockchain primitives are useful for by actually implementing and testing them, rather than collecting buzzwords.

title: Option Pricing Engine
short: A from-scratch Python/Streamlit options pricing engine comparing Black-Scholes, Monte Carlo and binomial-tree pricing — extended with Greeks, implied volatility, American options and a real-market IV surface.
problem: Options pricing libraries hide the numerical logic behind a single function call, which makes it hard to see why different models agree, where they diverge, and how a theoretical price holds up against real, messy market quotes.
approach: Implemented without a dedicated options-pricing library so every step is visible: Black-Scholes(-Merton) analytically with a continuous dividend yield, Monte Carlo under Geometric Brownian Motion with a standard error, and a Cox-Ross-Rubinstein binomial tree via backward induction — extended to American early exercise. On top sit Delta/Gamma/Vega/Theta, a bisection implied-volatility solver and put-call parity checks. A market-data layer then pulls option chains from Yahoo Finance (or a CSV) through a pluggable provider interface, normalizes them into one schema, applies liquidity filters and model-free no-arbitrage checks, solves implied volatility per contract and builds the volatility smile, a 3D IV surface and a flat-volatility calibration report.
result: An interactive Streamlit pricing lab backed by 33 pytest unit tests: price European or American calls and puts three ways, compare runtime and convergence, inspect Greeks and payoff, then load a real option chain to see its smile, IV surface and how far a constant-volatility model misses market prices (MAE / RMSE / MAPE). Built as a learning and research tool — not trading advice or a trading system.
tagline: Three ways to price the same option — and checking they agree.
pipeline: Inputs (S, K, T, r, σ, q)
highlights: Yahoo Finance or CSV option chains
details: The same option is priced three different ways on purpose: Black-Scholes is analytical and fast, Monte Carlo is flexible simulation-based pricing, and the binomial tree is an intuitive discrete-time framework that extends naturally to American early exercise. Convergence plots show the models meeting — Monte Carlo error shrinking as paths increase, the tree approaching Black-Scholes as steps increase — before the engine is pointed at real option chains.
learned: Convergence made the math tangible: Monte Carlo error shrinks statistically with more simulated paths, while the binomial tree steps toward the Black-Scholes value as the time step shrinks. Real option chains were the other lesson — zero bids, stale after-hours quotes and missing strikes mean most of the market-data work is filtering and diagnosing data, not pricing it.

title: Market Notebook
short: A personal research space for macro, crypto and market-structure observations.
problem: Market narratives move fast; writing down the thesis forces clearer thinking.
approach: Track liquidity, macro variables, crypto structure and competing bull/bear cases.
result: An evolving public research notebook rather than a signal-selling dashboard.
tagline: A public notebook for evolving market theses.
details: The notebook separates observations from conclusions. Every thesis should have a bull case, a bear case and a condition that would make the thesis wrong.
